## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

- **Any price amount.** Never published, at launch or since; the founder's $3 to $5 per pole is the operator's reading
  (item 7), and the header says so.
- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

founder.order_why: The recency question (screen 4) splits the context in two, so screen 5 comes back to the same context heading after the window has already been set, when the window would sit more naturally after all the context fields.

screens.why4: The coverage ladder fits, but 'Only some poles got checked' and 'Few poles got checked, many skipped' are close to each other, and no row covers poles that were reached but could not be seen properly, such as tops hidden from the ground.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my clipboard-and-binoculars foot patrol, but the bar names its threshold row two ways ('Most poles got checked, a few skipped' in the box, 'Most checked; a few skipped for access' in the saved text), so the line drifted between screen and record.
screens.instead: On the last circuit you patrolled, how many of its poles did you get a good look at? — Every one, top to bottom / Most, a few skipped or poorly seen / About half / Only a few / We never got to it

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer's voice just before the study goes out to linemen is where this choice belongs, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "linemans" is not a word anyone in the trade uses; it's "linemen", and the hint packs voice, video, typing, credits and text messages into one long read.
screens.why3: Choosing which voice my linemen hear is my own call as the founder, and I can make it after a 5-second listen.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a sample, and a preselected default covers the founder who doesn't care.
screens.why5: I typed "linemen who inspect poles at US power utilities" and the screen respells it "linemans", a small drift from my words though nothing of the product leaks.
screens.instead: Who should ask linemen your questions? (Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s) — one voice is recorded for this project, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Choosing how linemen will answer belongs right before the study is sent, after who asks the questions was settled.
screens.why2: "linemens" is a misspelled plural no one in the trade writes, so I have to read it twice, though the three formats are clear.
screens.why3: I know my linemen answer from a truck or a yard between jobs, often somewhere loud, so I can pick a format from what I know of them.
screens.why4: AI voice, read and tap, and let them choose are complete and distinct, and each one says when it is ready.
screens.why5: My word "linemen" comes back as "linemens", so the meaning holds but the word I typed has been mangled.
screens.instead: How should linemen answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud; they talk, type or tap) / Read and tap / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how linemen answer, deciding who receives the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen and clear enough in context.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching linemen I know by name at the co-ops and utilities we're piloting with, or posting to a group.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and cover the real routes, but the group option forces a Google sign-in that many linemen in a co-op crew room would balk at, and there's no mix of named people plus a posted link.
screens.why5: Nothing of my drones or pads leaks here, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — Linemen I know by name (one link each) / A list I found with Keel / One open link I post where linemen gather, like a lineman forum or co-op group (sign-in kept short)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it (Frequency: 3 answered), and each card spells out '3 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know why the stage isn't called.
screens.why_b2: There's no chart here, but the Prevalence line '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7' reads plainly; 'above your band' needs a second look, though, because my band was 6 to 7 in 10 and the bar is 5 of 7, so I have to work out how those relate.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution carry my belief lines word for word (foot patrol with binoculars and a clipboard, one of the two they'd most like made easier), and Prevalence and Frequency are my pole-by-pole-from-the-ground occasion over 3 months.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the screen never says why only 3 of the 7 linemen reached Frequency, Importance and Current solution, or whether to send more studies or re-ask, so I'm left guessing at the next move.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible everywhere (7 answered, 3 answered, 6 of 7), the thin cards are called too few rather than leaning either way, and 'among these 7' hedges the one holding card.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 3 of 7 linemen answered Frequency, Importance and Current solution (5 needed each) because 4 were not counted; get at least 2 more linemen who patrolled poles this quarter to answer before reading the problem.

screens.why_b1: The status "Holding up above your band" sits right beside its deciding numbers, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against over 7 people, with the marker at 5 on a 0-to-7 axis labelled as my bar, and I read all three at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it as my patrol circumstance, but I typed "checked one by one from the ground" for poles due on a circuit, and the card says "checked lines pole by pole" under a Prevalence band I never wrote as a belief.
screens.why_b4: "Common among these 7" plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me this card decides nothing alone, but not what it means for selling drone patrols to utilities.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and "a lean, not a call" are both visible, but "above your band" rests on a one-person margin and counts Ray's and Dale's guessed answers as a clean "said yes", so the result reads firmer than it is.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 linemen patrolled poles from the ground this quarter (bar 5), two of those yeses guessed from vague answers; a lean among 7, so read Frequency and Importance before leaning on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '3 counted, 5 needed', but the header says '3 answered' while the count line says 6 answered, so the deciding number disagrees with itself until I read further.
screens.why_b2: Months out of 3, the median at 2 and my bar at 2 of 3 are plain, but the strip has 5 cells for 6 people (Ray is missing), so how many it counts over takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: It is my Frequency belief in my words: checking lines pole by pole from the ground on 2 to 3 months out of 3.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not say I need two more counted answers or that re-asking the two guessed linemen would settle it.
screens.why_b5: 'A lean, not a call' hints at a direction from only 3 counted answers (2 for, 1 against), a soft overstatement next to 'too few to call', and '3 answered' hides that 6 replied.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 linemen answered, but only 3 gave a count you can use (2 at your 2 to 3 months, 1 below). Two answers read as guesses and Ray would rather not say. Get 2 more clear answers, or re-ask Travis and Dale for the months, before you lean on this.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside its number, but the verdict says "3 answered" while the count line says 6 answered and 3 counted, so I have to work out that it means 3 counted out of the 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 6 picks from 3 people and the bar reads 2 of 3, but the strip shows 2 for and 4 against, which counts picks rather than people, so I needed a second look to see that only Keisha actually counts against me.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line are the ones I checked, word for word, with my 'Checking every pole from the ground' named as the problem.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it does not tell me I need two more counted linemen, or that Travis's and Dale's answers were set aside as guesses and could be asked again.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the screen refuses to call it, but "a lean, not a call" hints at a direction from 3 people, and the strip's 4 against makes the result look worse than the 2 of 3 people actually counted.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 6 counted (2 for, 1 against), 5 needed, so get two more linemen to name a specific season, and note that Keisha's trouble calls and short crews compete with patrols.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, '3 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats it as 3 counted, 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The rungs and for/against are plain, but 'your bar · 2 of 3' with exactly 2 for looks at first like my bar was met, and the strip's 2 ghost cells don't match the 3 people not counted until I work out they mean the 2 more answers needed.
screens.why_b3: It is my belief word for word, foot patrol, binoculars, clipboard and falling short, with the same 2-in-3 bar against 'Most checked; a few skipped for access'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is true but generic; it doesn't tell me I need two more clear answers or that Travis's and Dale's guessed answers are the ones to chase.
screens.why_b5: With 3 counted it refuses to call it, says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and shows all 6 answers, including Keisha's full check against me, so nothing is overstated.
screens.instead: 2 of the 3 counted fell short and lean your way, but you need 5; get two more linemen, or Travis and Dale, to name their last patrol and this decides.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "3 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in, about checking every pole from the ground.
screens.why_b4: "5 needed to call it" implies I should get two more linemen to answer, but nothing says so, and nothing says what Keisha's against means for the pitch; my Current solution line also vanishes from this screen without a word.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (3 answered, 1 against, 1 asked why), the low n is named as too few, and one quote is shown as one person, not a trend.
screens.why_b6: Keisha's line that trouble calls and being a crew short run her week, and that patrols get done but take time, is new to me: the pain is staffing and time, not missed poles, which reframes my pitch toward covering for a short crew rather than catching what foot patrols miss.
screens.instead: Say: one lineman of three ranked trouble calls and short crews above pole checks, because patrols get done but eat crew time; get two more linemen to answer before reading Importance, and show why Current solution has no box here.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it's obvious why it's asked: it confirms I've actually walked a circuit lately before asking me to tell about one.
screens.why2: Checking lines pole by pole from the ground is just a ground patrol to me, so I'd answer it on first read or hearing.
screens.why3: Patrolling and checking poles from the ground is my job, so I know straight off whether I did it in the last 3 months.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the two chips don't fit a gate: 'I can't recall one particular ground check' answers a different question than whether I did one, and 'I'd rather not say' is a second escape the rules say shouldn't exist.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'checked one by one from the ground' and leaks nothing about any product or company.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's one short question and then 'Yes or no,' easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you do a ground patrol, checking poles one by one? Yes · No (no escape chips on the gate)

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to checking poles from the ground, asking how often I did it is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'In how many months' takes me a second read, because I think of patrol work in days or circuits walked rather than in months counted out of three.
screens.why3: I know whether I was out patrolling poles each month this summer, so I can answer it straight from my own work.
screens.why4: 1, 2 or 3 covers every case once I've said yes, the numbers don't overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the one way out.
screens.why5: It's still about checking poles one by one from the ground, in my words, and nothing about anybody's product shows up.
screens.why6: It's short, it's one question, and 'a number from 1 to 3, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, how many of those months were you out checking poles from the ground? 1 · 2 · All 3 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I walked the poles, it makes sense to ask which part of my season I'd most want made easier, though the switch from 'the last 3 months' to 'last season' is a small jump.
screens.why2: Trees on the lines, getting power back after storms, trouble calls and walking poles are all how we talk on the crew, so I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: All five are things I actually deal with in a season, so I can pick one from what I know.
screens.why4: 'Too few linemen' is a problem behind all the others rather than a job of its own, so it overlaps them, and writing up and reporting what I find on a pole, which is a big part of my day, is missing.
screens.why5: Nothing here sounds like somebody's product; it reads as my own work, and the pole-checking option is how I'd say it myself.
screens.why6: One short question and five short phrases I can hold in my head, with 'none of these' said once at the end.
screens.instead: Think of your last season on the lines. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping trees clear of the lines · Getting the power back on after storms · Answering outage and trouble calls · Checking every pole from the ground · Writing up and reporting what you find · None of these

screens.why1: After asking which part of the patrol I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how my last walk of the poles actually went.
screens.why2: Foot patrol is my word, but 'checking each pole by foot patrol with binoculars and a clipboard' is a mouthful, and a lot of us carry a tablet now, not a clipboard.
screens.why3: I walked a circuit last month and know exactly how many poles I got to and which ones I skipped.
screens.why4: The options mix two things: how I checked (walked or drove) and how much I got through, so 'checked from the truck' could also be 'only part of the list'; and 'nobody got out to those poles' doesn't fit a question about my own last ground check.
screens.why5: Binoculars and clipboard reads like somebody's picture of the job pinned onto the question rather than how I'd describe my own patrol, so it's drifted a little.
screens.why6: The question is long to hear once, and five options mixing method and coverage are hard to hold, though each one says cleanly.
screens.instead: Think of your last ground patrol. How much of the circuit did you get to? Every pole up close; most, a few skipped for access; some only from the truck; or only part of the circuit. Or say you can't recall.
